inputs.need:
I am the quality lead for a radiology department in an academic hospital that reads about 310,000 examinations a year. Our reports often recommend follow-up imaging for incidental findings: lung nodules on chest CT, adrenal and renal lesions on abdominal CT, thyroid nodules on neck imaging, and pancreatic cysts. A spot check last spring of 200 reports with such a recommendation found that follow-up imaging had been done within the recommended window for 94 patients, and for 41 patients nobody could tell us whether the recommendation had even been seen. Two patients were later found to have cancers in lesions that had been flagged years earlier.

The department wants to choose a tracking approach before next year's budget round. The options on the table are structured recommendation codes in the report, a nurse navigator who follows up every flagged finding, automatic alerts to the ordering clinician in the electronic health record, letters sent directly to patients, or some combination. Each option has champions, and each needs money and staff.

Before we decide, I want a narrative review of how health systems track follow-up recommendations for incidental imaging findings: which approaches have been described, what follow-up completion they report, where the loop tends to break (the ordering clinician has left, the patient was seen only in the emergency department, the recommendation was vague), and who falls through the cracks. I am especially worried about patients without a family doctor and patients seen only in the emergency department. I need help framing the review question, choosing sources, and presenting conflicting reports to the department's quality committee without overselling any single system.
inputs.constraints: Three months for the review, reporting to the quality committee on 14 January 2027. Two radiologists and the hospital librarian share the work; no funding and no access to patient records for this review. English and French publications only.

records.title: Structured follow-up recommendation codes in radiology reports and completion of recommended imaging: a before-after study
records.authors: Haddad-Lindqvist S, Okonkwo-Pierce M, Tanaka-Brandt L
records.abstract: After our department introduced standard codes for follow-up recommendations in radiology reports, we compared 1,200 reports with an incidental finding before the change with 1,200 reports after it. Recommendations became more specific: the share naming a modality and an interval rose from 46 percent to 88 percent. Completion of recommended imaging within the stated interval rose from 51 percent to 58 percent. Completion was lowest for findings reported on emergency department examinations. The codes did not by themselves notify anyone, and completion was measured only within our own health system, so imaging done elsewhere was missed.

records.title: A nurse navigator for incidental pulmonary nodules: follow-up completion over three years
records.abstract: A nurse navigator reviewed every chest CT report with an incidental pulmonary nodule and a follow-up recommendation, contacted the ordering clinician and, when needed, the patient, and booked the follow-up scan. Over three years, 2,406 patients were tracked. Follow-up completion within the recommended window was 79 percent, compared with 43 percent in the year before the navigator started. Completion was 64 percent among patients without a regular primary care clinician. The navigator post required one full-time position for about 800 new nodules a year. The comparison was with a single earlier year and did not adjust for changes in referral patterns.

records.title: Automated alerts to ordering clinicians for actionable incidental findings: a controlled comparison across two hospitals
records.authors: Lorenz-Adeyemi K, Whitcombe-Nakashima P, Oduya-Grant F
records.abstract: One hospital sent an automated electronic health record alert to the ordering clinician for every report with an actionable incidental finding, while a sister hospital did not. Among 3,150 findings, follow-up was completed within the recommended interval for 62 percent at the alert hospital and 55 percent at the comparison hospital. Alerts were acknowledged within seven days for 71 percent of findings. When the ordering clinician was an emergency physician or a resident who had since rotated, acknowledgement fell to 38 percent. The hospitals differed in patient mix and in access to primary care.

records.title: Letters sent directly to patients about incidental imaging findings: effect on follow-up and on patient worry
records.abstract: Patients with an incidental finding that needed follow-up imaging were sent a plain-language letter by the radiology department in addition to the usual report to their clinician. Compared with a matched group from the previous year, follow-up completion rose from 48 percent to 60 percent. In a questionnaire returned by 212 of 390 patients who received letters, 17 percent said the letter made them very worried, and most said they would have preferred to hear about the finding from their own clinician. Letters were sent only in English, and patients without a fixed address were not reached.

records.title: Why follow-up of incidental imaging findings fails: a structured review of reported failure points
records.authors: Petit-Ramirez J, Soto-Lindgren E, Adu-Hargreave N
records.abstract: We reviewed 37 published reports of follow-up failures for incidental imaging findings and classified where the loop broke. The most frequent failure points were a recommendation that did not reach a clinician who took responsibility, vague recommendations without a modality or interval, patients seen only in emergency or inpatient settings without a follow-up clinician, and loss of contact after patients moved. Few reports described failures among patients who did not speak the local language. Most reports came from single academic centres, and the review did not assess the quality of the included reports.

records.title: Follow-up completion for incidental adrenal and renal lesions among patients without a primary care clinician
records.abstract: Among 1,038 patients with an incidental adrenal or renal lesion that needed follow-up imaging, 612 had a primary care clinician on record. Follow-up completion within one year was 67 percent for patients with a primary care clinician and 34 percent for those without. Patients first imaged in the emergency department made up most of those without a clinician. Completion was also lower among patients living in the most deprived neighbourhoods. The study used one health system's records and could not capture imaging done elsewhere, so completion may be underestimated for patients who moved.

records.title: Combining report codes, a tracking list and navigators for incidental findings: five years at a regional health system
records.authors: Quist-Ferreira H, Nwosu-Blake G, Holm-Achterberg I
records.abstract: A regional health system combined structured recommendation codes, a tracking list of every open recommendation, and two navigators who closed the loop with clinicians and patients. Over five years, 14,820 recommendations were tracked. Completion within the recommended interval rose from 49 percent in the first year to 76 percent in the fifth year. The programme needed 2.5 full-time staff, mostly navigator time and list maintenance. The system was introduced in stages alongside other safety work, so the contribution of each component cannot be separated, and there was no comparison health system.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Approaches that assign a person to close the loop report the largest gains (a navigator: 79 against 43 percent), clinician alerts help less when the ordering clinician is no longer responsible (acknowledgement 38 percent for emergency physicians and rotated residents), and letters to patients raise completion while worrying some patients. Patients without a primary care clinician complete follow-up far less often (34 against 67 percent), and the loop breaks at predictable points. Completion is defined with different windows and denominators, so figures cannot be pooled. The four model leads, including a national benchmark presented as a landmark, were not retrieved and are not part of this appraisal.
response.gradeRationale: Before-after and two-site comparisons from single systems, a structured review without quality assessment, and descriptive records; consistent in direction but at serious risk of bias and not comparable across definitions.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty low; the leads are not appraised.

steps.note: Appraisal of the seven retrieved records only; the leads are not annotated and no claim cites them. Applied through the appraisal mapper on the production scan path (S13), with the leads kept after the records (D1). The landmark lead is still unverified.

response.reading: The loop has five links: the recommendation is written, reaches a responsible clinician, is acknowledged, is acted on, and the follow-up is completed. Retrieved records show that codes improve the first link, alerts depend on the second, navigators and tracking lists repair the middle of the chain, and letters bypass the clinician at the cost of some worry. Patients without a primary care clinician and emergency-only patients break the chain at the second link. A model lead offering a national benchmark is not part of the evidence until it is checked.

response.theoreticalFramework: A closed-loop communication model (recommendation, receipt, acknowledgement, action, completion) organises the failure points; no other framework.
response.summary: Three-month narrative review; one primary outcome with its definition, one secondary, one process and one balancing measure.

response.designSummary: Narrative synthesis organised by failure point and approach; completion figures tabulated with their definitions and never pooled.
response.sampleSize: Not applicable: the unit is the published report. The pre-search retrieved seven relevant records, one of them a structured review of 37 reports, so about 40 to 60 eligible reports are expected; the synthesis describes ranges and patterns rather than a pooled estimate.
response.primaryAnalysis: For each approach, a table of completion with and without the approach, with window, denominator, finding types, setting and design; patterns across approaches described without vote counting.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Failure points mapped to the approaches that address them; results for patients without a primary care clinician, emergency-only patients and patients who need an interpreter reported wherever available; resources per approach where reported.
response.missingData: Reports without a completion denominator are described but left out of the completion table; missing subgroup results are recorded as not reported.
response.multiplicity: No statistical testing; approaches are not ranked by significance.
response.software: Reference manager and a shared extraction spreadsheet.
overfittingGuards: No pooling of completion figures with different windows or denominators
Every figure cited to the committee checked against its source record
Unverified leads listed separately and never cited as evidence
response.summary: Narrative synthesis without pooling; the number and comparability of reports, not a power calculation, limit what can be concluded.

response.risks: No patients are involved; the risks are overselling one approach and anchoring the committee on an unverified figure.
response.consent: Not applicable; no patient data are used for the review.
response.data: Published and publicly available reports only; the spring spot check is described with the department's aggregate figures and no patient identifiers.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients without a primary care clinician, emergency-only patients, patients who need an interpreter and patients in the most deprived neighbourhoods complete follow-up less often. The review extracts results for these groups wherever reported, and the committee report states which approaches were never tested with them.
response.effectiveness: The committee gets a comparison of approaches with their definitions, settings, resources and blind spots instead of competing single figures.
response.efficiency: Two radiologists and three librarian days; the review may prevent spending on an approach that misses the patients most at risk.
response.costs: Staff time within existing roles; no direct costs.
response.grants: None needed; an evaluation of the chosen approach could later seek hospital quality funding.
response.partnerships: Hospital librarian, an emergency physician, a primary care representative and a patient partner who comments on how findings should be communicated.
response.rebPath: A literature review needs no research ethics review; the chair approved it as departmental quality work. Any later evaluation of the chosen approach that uses patient records will go through the hospital's ethics screening.
response.limitations: Narrative synthesis, English and French reports only, mostly single-centre before-after evidence, and completion definitions that differ.
response.summary: No participants; the ethical weight lies in honest comparison, attention to the patients most often missed, and keeping unverified figures out.

response.partnershipPlan: A patient partner, an emergency physician and a primary care representative comment on the review question and on the committee summary before it is sent.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the hospital's patient relations log is read for complaints about findings that were not followed up.

response.title: Tracking follow-up of incidental imaging findings: a narrative review of approaches, failure points and the patients who are missed
response.abstract: Background: follow-up imaging recommended for incidental findings is often not done. Aim: to describe approaches used to track these recommendations, the completion they report, where the loop breaks and which patients are missed. Methods: narrative review of reports from 2010 to 2026 in English and French, organised by failure point, with completion figures reported with their definitions and not pooled. Results and conclusions will be written after the review.
response.introduction: Incidental findings are common, and follow-up recommendations often go unacted. Departments can choose report codes, tracking lists, navigators, clinician alerts or letters to patients, but these have been studied in different settings with different definitions of completion.
response.methods: Three bibliographic databases and grey literature searched, with citation follow-up. Two radiologists screen and extract approach, setting, finding types, completion definition, failure points, resources and results for patients without a primary care clinician, emergency-only patients and patients who need an interpreter. Figures are checked against their sources; unverified leads are excluded.
response.results: No review data have been extracted yet. The report will present the flow of reports, a table of approaches with completion and definitions, the failure points each approach addresses, resources, and results for the groups most often missed.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare approaches by the links of the loop they repair, weigh the quality and comparability of the evidence, and state what it means for the department's choice.
response.limitations: Narrative synthesis; English and French reports only; mostly single-centre before-after evidence; completion defined differently across reports.
response.conclusion: To be written after the review; it will not rank approaches by a pooled figure and will cite no unverified benchmark.
response.reportingChecklist: SANRA items as a quality checklist for narrative reviews
response.summary: Narrative review draft with results left empty until extraction is complete.
